title: Speaking up
hookLine: Thoreau goes to jail rather than pay a tax that backs slavery; Emerson keeps to the inner life, then speaks out: conscience, voiced
tomorrow: why did an old man haul river water before dawn, unseen?

lines: A ROOM LOOKING AT THE TABLE.
THE TRUE PLACE FOR A JUST MAN.
cards: A meeting, a cruel remark, and a whole room looking down at the table. Henry David Thoreau, in Concord, refused to pay his poll tax. He wouldn't fund a government that upheld slavery and was waging a war he called unjust.
So he spent a night in jail. In his essay he puts it plainly: "Under a government which imprisons any unjustly, the true place for a just man is also a prison."

teach.b: His friend Ralph Waldo Emerson stood somewhere else. Emerson's case: real change starts inside, with the self, not with crusades. In Self-Reliance he bristles at being told to fix every poor man's lot: "Are they my poor?"
A well-known story, probably legend, has Emerson at the jail asking, Henry, what are you doing in there? And Thoreau answering, Waldo, what are you doing out there? Hear both.

Thoreau: "Must the citizen ever for a moment, or in the least degree, resign his conscience to the legislator?" Conscience can't be handed off. If a law makes you an agent of wrong, break it openly and take the penalty.
Emerson: causes and noise can pull a person away from their own true work, and the deepest reform is inward.
Both stand inside one teaching, the Transcendentalist trust in conscience, the voice within each person, above the crowd. Then the turn.
When the Fugitive Slave Law required Northerners to help return people escaping slavery, Emerson spoke against it in public, and wrote in his journal that he would not obey it.
The man of the study found his voice. For the Transcendentalists, that's speaking up: conscience is your own, and when it's clear, it comes out loud.

how: Readers of Thoreau's essay on civil disobedience and of Emerson's addresses take from them a practice of examining conscience and, when it is clear, saying so publicly and accepting the cost.

o: posting your opinion on every issue

games.q: conscience in Concord: tap the pairs.
p: a night in jail over the poll tax
Emerson wrote he would not obey it

s: Thoreau quietly paid the tax and wrote about it later
he refused it and spent a night in jail; his essay says someone else paid it.
the jail-visit exchange between Emerson and Thoreau is well documented
it's a well-known story, probably legend.
Emerson, who favored the inward life, later spoke out in public against a law
he spoke against the Fugitive Slave Law and wrote that he would not obey it.

games.q: your friend says protests are pointless and real change is inner work. before you answer, what is the strongest version of her view, in Emerson's terms?
o: outer causes can pull a person from their true work; change starts in the self
she just doesn't care about anyone but herself
she's afraid of getting in trouble, that's all
games.why: that's Emerson's real case. Thoreau's answer is that conscience can't be handed to anyone. say hers first, at its best, then yours.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you've stayed quiet about that your conscience is clear on. Find the one sentence you'd say about it, and say it once, softly, out loud. Then sit with how it sounds in your own voice until the sit ends.

wordCard.voice: Speaking up: the Transcendentalist trust in conscience, voiced, whether from a jail cell like Thoreau or, in time, from a public stage like Emerson.

carryVoice: Keep this: speak up, when your conscience is clear and the room goes quiet. See you tomorrow.
